title: Why Silence Is Harder Than It Looks (And Worth It)
meta_description: Silence and solitude in the Bible aren't about feeling calm. Here's why sitting still is so hard for men, and a practical way to start anyway.
body_markdown:
## The first two minutes are the worst

Most men who try to sit in silence before reading Scripture quit inside two minutes. Not because nothing happens, but because too much does.

You sit down. You close the laptop. And your mind immediately produces a to-do list, an argument you lost three years ago, a half-remembered email, and a strong urge to check your phone. Silence doesn't feel peaceful. It feels like standing in a room where every appliance has started running at once.

That noise was always there. Silence just stops covering it up.

## Why the Bible keeps pairing silence and solitude

When people search for what the Bible says about silence and solitude, they often expect a promise of calm. That's not quite what's there.

Elijah, in 1 Kings 19, runs to Horeb exhausted and afraid. God shows up not in the wind, the earthquake, or the fire, but in what the text describes as a low whisper — and Elijah has to be quiet enough to notice it. In Mark 1:35, Jesus gets up while it's still dark and goes to a solitary place to pray, and the disciples have to come find him. Habakkuk 2:20 tells the whole earth to keep silence before the Lord.

None of these are about feeling relaxed. They're about removing enough input that you can actually hear.

Silence in Scripture is less a mood and more a clearing. You stop generating noise so that something other than your own voice has a chance to register.

## What the discomfort is actually telling you

Here's the part most advice skips: the agitation you feel in silence is information.

If you can't sit still for three minutes without reaching for a screen, that tells you something about how much of your day is spent being managed by input rather than choosing it. If your mind floods with unfinished conflicts, that tells you what's unresolved. If you feel bored almost instantly, that tells you how conditioned you've become to constant stimulus.

None of that is a failure. It's the diagnostic. You can't fix what you never let surface.

This is also why gamified approaches tend to work against you here. A streak counter or a badge pulls your attention right back to the meter. It converts silence into a task to complete rather than a space to enter. You end up watching yourself be silent instead of being silent.

## A practical way to start

You don't need a retreat or a cabin. You need a small, repeatable pattern that doesn't depend on how you feel.

**Pick a fixed length, and keep it short.** Three minutes is plenty at first. Set a timer so you aren't tempted to check. Knowing the end is fixed removes the low-level anxiety of not knowing when you're done.

**Sit before you read, not after.** Reading first tends to fill your head with more to think about. Silence first empties it a little so the text has somewhere to land.

**Don't try to stop thinking.** When the noise comes, let it come. Notice it, name it if that helps — "that's the work thing," "that's the argument" — and let it pass. You're not clearing your mind. You're declining to chase.

**Then read one short passage.** Not a chapter. A few verses. Read it twice, slowly. Stop.

This is roughly how Selah is built: a short silence, a single passage, and then nothing else pulling at you. No streak to protect, no progress bar. The design is there to remove reasons to look at the screen, not add them.

## It gets easier, but not in the way you expect

After a few weeks, the first two minutes are still noisy. That part doesn't really change.

What changes is your relationship to the noise. You stop treating it as evidence that you're doing this wrong. You start seeing it as the normal weather of a mind that has been running hot all day. You wait it out. Some days something quiet comes through underneath. Many days nothing obvious does.

That's fine. Elijah didn't get the whisper on demand either. He got it because he was standing still when it came.

The point of silence and solitude isn't the feeling it produces. It's the posture it creates: a man who has stopped talking long enough to be spoken to. That posture is worth building even on the days it feels like nothing.

Especially on those days.
